description: The deterministic projection from the selected XNA contract to Common Lisp. tools/api-compat/verify.py applies these rules to the live image; docs/common-lisp-mapping.md is the prose that explains them.

naming.identifier: A CLR identifier becomes a Lisp symbol by inserting a hyphen at each case boundary and lowercasing. Texture2D becomes texture-2d, because the D after the digit starts a new word; Bgra4444 becomes bgra4444, because nothing does. That is the same rule the generated ABI constants already follow.
naming.reference_type_member: <member>, in the type's package, as a generic function or reader.
naming.value_type_member: <type>-<member>, in the type's package. The prefix is what keeps Rectangle's Left from colliding with Viewport's.
naming.static_class_member: <class>-<member>, so that Mouse and GamePad can join Keyboard's namespace without collision.
naming.constructor: make-instance for a reference type; make-<type> for a value type.
naming.enum_member: a keyword named by the identifier rule; the exact value is preserved in the runtime table.

OnExiting(Object,EventArgs).reason: The CLR event-handler pattern passes a sender and an argument object. A CLOS method on the game needs neither: the game is the receiver, and the exiting notification carries nothing else.

Activated.reason: A CLR event is two operations, add_E and remove_E, and it projects to two generic functions on the object that raises it. They are generic because Disposed is raised by more than one type in this package and a plain function could not be specialised on the second. The handler takes the sender and nothing else: EventArgs.Empty carries no information, and a second always-empty argument would be something every handler had to write and ignore.

not_applicable.Dispose(Boolean): The protected dispose(bool) pattern; see Game.Dispose(Boolean).

DeviceCreated.reason: The same projection Game's events use, over cna_graphics_device_manager_subscribe. CNA gives manager registrations the same handle type and the same release route as the game's, so one mechanism serves both.

unimplemented.PreparingDeviceSettings: The only event in the selection that carries data. It needs PreparingDeviceSettingsEventArgs and GraphicsDeviceInformation, neither of which is in the selection, and CNA's non-ext callback for it can only observe the settings where XNA's event exists to change them. Projecting the observing form under the event's name would be a quieter kind of wrong than leaving it missing.

.ctor.reason: XNA tells the integer and float constructors apart by static type, and Common Lisp would have to tell 1 from 1.0 at run time to do the same. Those two mean almost opposite colours -- (make-color 1 1 1) is very nearly black where (make-color-from-floats 1.0 1.0 1.0) is white -- so the distinction is a name here rather than a numeric type nobody can see. FromNonPremultiplied.reason: The two overloads are different computations, not one operation reached two ways: the integer form truncates an integer quotient and the Vector4 form multiplies in floats and packs through PackUNorm. They disagree by a level on ordinary inputs, so collapsing them would hide a real difference.

Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Color.predefined_value_reason: XNA's 141 predefined colours are static properties on a value type. A Lisp constant would be wrong for all of them, because Color is mutable and every read of the original is a copy.

Name.reason: A member whose bare projected name would collide across the package takes the type prefix, as Texture.Format does. NAME alone would meet every other named thing in the graphics package.

IsDisposed.reason: Asks CNA rather than the CLOS object, so a resource CNA disposed underneath the binding reports disposed even before the Lisp side notices. DISPOSED-P is the CNA-Lisp question and answers the same thing for every live object.

Tag.reason: XNA's Tag is System.Object -- arbitrary consumer data the framework never reads. CNA's is a uint64 token, which cannot hold a Lisp object and could only hold a pointer to one, and putting a pointer to a moving object into C is the thing this binding never does. So the tag is a Lisp slot and is not round-tripped through the C ABI.

GraphicsDevice.reason: Answers the game's GRAPHICS-DEVICE facade. There is one device in a CNA-Lisp program and two objects for it would be one too many; the C handle CNA answers here is a borrowed, callback-scoped one like every other.

Dispose().reason: Every native object in this binding already carries deterministic disposal. GraphicsResource does not introduce a second mechanism: Dispose() is DISPOSE, which is a declared extension because XNA spells disposal differently on each type that has it.

Disposing.reason: The same projection the other events use. A resource registration is its own handle type with its own release route, unlike the game's and the manager's, which share one.

Viewport.reason: The reader is unconditional. The setter goes through the optional private shim: cna_graphics_device_set_viewport takes CNA_Viewport by value, and the System V AMD64 ABI passes a 24-byte aggregate in memory, which CFFI cannot do without cffi-libffi. The shim is not shipped prebuilt -- a release must load with no C toolchain -- so a consumer that has not built it gets a CNA-NOT-SUPPORTED-ERROR naming CNA_LISP_SHIM and the command that produces one. The qualified configuration includes the shim and exercises the setter.
